6.text: Nutritional value of proteins and protein deficiency

The daily protein requirement for adults is **0.8–1 g/kg** body weight; in pregnancy, lactation, periods of growth, severe illness and burns it rises to 1.2–2 g/kg. Animal proteins (eggs, milk, meat, fish) contain all the essential amino acids and are well digested; plant proteins are low in some of them (lysine in cereals, methionine in legumes).

parts.text: In kwashiorkor the liver cannot export triglycerides because it lacks protein (apoproteins) for lipoprotein synthesis — a **fatty liver** develops. The edema is explained by the fall in albumin and oncotic pressure (topic 2).

insert.title: 0. Amino acid metabolism, nitrogen balance and ammonia

blocks.text: Proteins are constantly renewed in the body: in adults ≈ 300–400 g of protein is broken down and resynthesized daily. The nitrogen of the released amino acids is excreted mainly as **urea** in the urine. The ratio of nitrogen taken in with food to nitrogen excreted is called the **nitrogen balance** (≈ 16 % of protein mass is nitrogen, i.e. nitrogen · 6.25 = protein).

items: **Positive nitrogen balance** (intake > output): growth, pregnancy, recovery from illness, increase in muscle mass.
**Negative nitrogen balance** (output > intake): starvation, burns, severe infections and operations, cancer cachexia, treatment with glucocorticoids.

blocks.text: **Transaminases** are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid (coenzyme — pyridoxal phosphate): **ALT** (alanine aminotransferase, mainly in the liver) and **AST** (aspartate aminotransferase, in the liver, heart and skeletal muscles). When cells are damaged they are released into the blood; the normal level of each is up to ≈ 40 U/L. The **De Ritis ratio** (AST / ALT ≈ 1.3) helps to estimate the site of damage: < 1 in viral hepatitis (ALT predominates), > 2 in alcoholic liver damage and myocardial infarction.

**Ammonia** (NH~3~), formed in the deamination of amino acids, is a potent neurotoxin: in the brain it binds α-ketoglutarate into glutamate and glutamine, slowing the Krebs cycle, and causes osmotic swelling of astrocytes. In the liver ammonia is converted into harmless urea in the **urea cycle**: 2NH~3~ + CO~2~ → (NH~2~)~2~CO + H~2~O (ATP is consumed in the cycle). The normal blood ammonia level is < 50 µmol/L.

parts.text: **Hepatic encephalopathy:** in cirrhosis or acute liver failure urea synthesis decreases and ammonia accumulates in the blood — drowsiness, confusion, “flapping” tremor (asterixis), coma. **Lactulose** is used in treatment: in the colon it is broken down by bacteria into lactic and acetic acids and acidifies the contents; NH~3~ becomes ionized to NH~4~^+^, is not absorbed into the blood and is excreted in the feces.

insert.title: 0. Fibrous proteins and disorders of protein folding

blocks.text: **Collagen** is the most abundant protein in the body (≈ 25–30 % of total protein). Each of its chains contains repeating **Gly−X−Y** (X is often proline, Y — hydroxyproline or hydroxylysine); three left-handed chains form a right-handed **triple helix**. Only the smallest amino acid — glycine — fits inside the helix. The enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine require **ascorbic acid** (vitamin C) and Fe^2+^; the hydrogen bonds of hydroxyproline stabilize the triple helix.

Correct protein folding in the cell is assisted by **chaperones** (heat shock proteins). Misfolded proteins are usually degraded in the proteasome; if they accumulate and form insoluble β-sheet fibrils, **amyloidosis** and neurodegenerative diseases develop.

items: Determine the daily protein intake (from the diet or parenteral nutrition).
Calculate the nitrogen intake: N~in~ = protein (g) / 6.25.
Determine the urea nitrogen (g) in the daily urine and add ≈ 4 g for other losses through urine, feces and skin: N~out~ = urea nitrogen + 4.
Find the nitrogen balance: NB = N~in~ − N~out~.
Assess the result: positive — anabolism, negative — protein catabolism; with a negative balance an increase in dietary protein is planned.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: An elderly man living alone who for a long time ate only bread, potatoes and tea has bleeding, swollen gums, loose teeth, pinpoint hemorrhages in the skin, and small wounds that heal slowly.
cases.ask: Deficiency of which vitamin? Explain the molecular cause of the signs in terms of collagen structure.
cases.answer: This is **scurvy** — **vitamin C** deficiency. Ascorbic acid is required for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases: it keeps the iron of the enzyme in the Fe^2+^ state. Without vitamin C, proline and lysine in collagen chains are not hydroxylated and the hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds do not form — the **triple helix is unstable** and collagen fibers are fragile. As a result the vessel walls weaken (hemorrhages, bleeding gums), the periodontal ligament loosens and wounds do not heal. Treatment — vitamin C and a diet rich in fruit and vegetables.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: Blood tests of two patients: the first has ALT 820 U/L, AST 610 U/L and jaundice; the second has ALT 60 U/L, AST 180 U/L and a history of many years of alcohol use.
cases.ask: Calculate the De Ritis ratio for each patient and assess the nature of the damage.
cases.answer: Patient 1: AST / ALT = 610 / 820 ≈ **0.74** (< 1) — ALT predominates, the cytoplasm of liver cells is massively damaged; this is typical of **acute viral hepatitis**. Patient 2: 180 / 60 = **3** (> 2) — AST predominates; part of AST is located in mitochondria, which alcohol damages, and in addition B~6~ deficiency in alcoholism reduces ALT synthesis — typical of **alcoholic liver damage**. In both cases the diagnosis is confirmed by other tests.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A patient with severe burns receives 75 g of protein a day by parenteral nutrition. The daily urine contains 18 g of urea nitrogen.
cases.ask: Calculate and assess the nitrogen balance.
cases.answer: N~in~ = 75 / 6.25 = **12 g**. N~out~ = 18 + 4 = **22 g**. Nitrogen balance = 12 − 22 = **−10 g/day** — sharply negative. In burns, stress hormones cause rapid breakdown of muscle proteins, and protein is also lost from the burn surface. Each 1 g of nitrogen corresponds to ≈ 6.25 g of protein or ≈ 30 g of muscle tissue, so the patient is losing ≈ 300 g of muscle a day. The protein intake should be increased to 1.5–2 g/kg.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A 2-year-old child weaned early from breast milk and fed mainly rice porridge has swollen legs and face, a large abdomen, sparse discolored hair and is apathetic. Blood albumin is 18 g/L.
cases.ask: What is the condition? Explain the biochemical cause of the edema and the enlarged abdomen.
cases.answer: This is **kwashiorkor** — enough energy (carbohydrate) but a severe lack of protein. The liver cannot synthesize enough albumin — albumin is 18 g/L, the **oncotic pressure has fallen**, and water stays in the tissues — edema and ascites. Because apoproteins are lacking, the liver cannot export triglycerides as lipoproteins — a **fatty liver** enlarges, and the abdomen looks big. Treatment: feeding with milk-based therapeutic formulas, increasing protein and energy gradually, and treating infections.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A patient with liver cirrhosis became drowsy and confused after bleeding from esophageal varices; there is a “flapping” tremor of the hands. Blood ammonia is 140 µmol/L (normal < 50).
cases.ask: How did the bleeding cause the rise in ammonia? How does lactulose help?
cases.answer: Blood in the intestine is a large amount of **protein**: bacteria break it down and produce a lot of **ammonia**. In cirrhosis the liver cannot detoxify ammonia in the urea cycle, and in addition blood bypasses the portal system — ammonia reaches the brain and causes **hepatic encephalopathy**. **Lactulose** is broken down by bacteria in the colon into organic acids, and the contents become acidic: NH~3~ + H^+^ → NH~4~^+^; ionized ammonium is not absorbed into the blood and is excreted in the feces, while the laxative effect of lactulose cleans out the intestine. In addition, an antibiotic that reduces intestinal bacteria (rifaximin) is given.

cards.back: Difference between nitrogen intake and output; protein = nitrogen · 6.25; positive in growth, negative in burns and starvation
AST / ALT ≈ 1.3; < 1 in hepatitis, > 2 in alcoholic damage and infarction
A neurotoxin; detoxified in the liver in the urea cycle; normal < 50 µmol/L
Gly−X−Y repeats, triple helix; vitamin C is needed to hydroxylate proline
Proteins that help other proteins fold correctly (heat shock proteins)
Protein deficiency: edema, fatty liver, low albumin; no edema in marasmus
